(<reference osisRef="Isa.49.26">Is 49:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.15-Jer.25.29">Jr 25:15-29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.12.2">Zec 12:2</reference>).<div eID="gen16004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16005" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Bow down that ... go over--</hi>Conquerors often literally trod on the necks of conquered kings, as Sapor of Persia did to the Roman emperor Valerian (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.24">Jos 10:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.40">Psa 18:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.66.11">66:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.12">12</reference>). <chapter eID="Isa.51"/>

entries.117f21c8d7fd63a316ce2275ad8e69d1a64fcbac: <div eID="gen28526" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen28527" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28528" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28528" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28527" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28529" type="x-p"/> The prophet exhorts the children of Abraham to trust in the Lord; and briefly, but beautifully, describes the great blessedness which should be the consequence, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.1-Isa.51.3">Isa 51:1-3</reference>. Then, turning to the Gentiles, encourages them to look for a portion in the same salvation, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.4">Isa 51:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.5">Isa 51:5</reference>; the everlasting duration of which is majestically described, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.6">Isa 51:6</reference>. And as it is everlasting, so is it sure to the righteous, notwithstanding all the machinations of their enemies, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.7">Isa 51:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.8">Isa 51:8</reference>. The faithful, then, with exultation and joy, lift their voices, reminding God of his wondrous works of old, which encourage them to look now for the like glorious accomplishment of these promises, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.9-Isa.51.11">Isa 51:9-11</reference>. In answer to this the Divinity is introduced comforting them under their trials, and telling them that the deliverer was already on his way to save and to establish them, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.12-Isa.51.16">Isa 51:12-16</reference>. On this the prophet turns to Jerusalem to comfort and congratulate her on so joyful a prospect. She is represented, by a bold image, as a person lying in the streets, under the intoxicating effects of the cup of the Divine wrath, without a single person from among her own people appointed to give her consolation, and trodden under the feet of her enemies; but, in the time allotted by the Divine providence, the cup of trembling shall be taken out of her hand, and put into that of her oppressors; and she shall drink it no more again for ever, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.17-Isa.51.22">Isa 51:17-22</reference>. <div eID="gen28529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28530" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen28530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28531" type="x-p"/> Ye that follow after righteousness - The people who, feeling the want of salvation, seek the Lord in order to be justified. <div eID="gen28531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28532" type="x-p"/> The rock - Abraham. <div eID="gen28532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28533" type="x-p"/> The hole of the pit - Sarah; as explained in <reference osisRef="Isa.51.2">Isa 51:2</reference>.
entries.dc8376ecb0ddf3b5fcc98116c5f1ef1c19c38c4b: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen28533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28534" type="x-p"/> I called him alone - As I have made out of one a great nation; so, although ye are brought low and minished, yet I can restore you to happiness, and greatly multiply your number.
entries.dc1949a0ff9c4aeee045449d5bee4d222a07bcee: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen28534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28535" type="x-p"/> By people - O my nation "O ye peoples - O ye nations" - For עמי ammi, my people, the Bodleian MS. and another read עמים ammim, ye peoples; and for לאומי leumi, my nation, the Bodleian MS. and eight others, (two of them ancient), and four of De Rossi's, read לאמים leummim, ye nations; and so the Syriac in both words. The difference is very material; for in this case the address is made not to the Jews, but to the Gentiles, as in all reason it ought to be; for this and the two following verses express the call of the Gentiles, the islands, or the distant lands on the coasts of the Mediterranean and other seas. It is also to be observed that God in no other place calls his people לאמי leummi, my nation. It has been before remarked that transcribers frequently omitted the final מ mem of nouns plural, and supplied it, for brevity's sake, and sometimes for want of room at the end of a line, by a small stroke thus /עמי; which mark, being effaced or overlooked, has been the occasion of many mistakes of this kind. <div eID="gen28535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28536" type="x-p"/> A law shall proceed from me - The new law, the Gospel of our Lord Jesus. Kimchi says, "After the war with Gog and Magog the King Messiah will teach the people to walk in the ways of the Lord."
entries.d2117ed945488a98c6675a56c79bf329d1f380c7: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen28536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28537" type="x-p"/> My righteousness is near - The word צדק tsedek, righteousness, is used in such a great latitude of signification, for justice, truth, faithfulness, goodness, mercy, deliverance, salvation, etc., that it is not easy sometimes to give the precise meaning of it without much circumlocution; it means here the faithful completion of God's promises to deliver his people.
entries.ed9276ef403ce73371799fa976a6ca5351d4f255: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen28537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28538" type="x-p"/> My salvation shall be for ever - Aben Ezra says, From this verse divines have learnt the immortality of the soul. Men shall perish as the earth does, because they are formed from it; but they who are filled with the salvation of God shall remain for ever. See Kimchi.
entries.a0fdf4b119d85551dde9c9ece1063e879bb53ef4: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen28538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28539" type="x-p"/> They shall obtain gladness and joy, and sorrow and mourning shall flee away - Nineteen MSS. and the two oldest editions have ישגו yasigu; and forty-six MSS. of Kennicott's and ten of De Rossi's, and the same two editions, and agreeably to them the Chaldee and Syriac, have ונסו venasu; and so both words are expressed, <reference osisRef="Isa.35.10">Isa 35:10</reference>, of which place this is a repetition. And from comparing both together it appears that the ו vau in this place is become by mistake in the present text final, nun of the preceding word.
entries.9ea81a0f7f9610b8ac7f0f49e634898f3306bb2e: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen28539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28540" type="x-p"/> Of the oppressor, as if he, etc. - "The כ caph in כאשר keasher seems clearly to have changed its situation from the end of the preceding word to the beginning of this; or rather, to have been omitted by mistake there, because it was here. That it was there the Septuagint show by rendering המציקך hammetsikech θλιβοντος σε, of him, that oppressed thee. And so they render this word in both its places in this verse. The Vulgate also has the pronoun in the first instance; furoris ejus qui te tribulabat." Dr. Jubb. The correction seems well founded; I have not conformed the translation to it, because it makes little difference in the sense.
entries.f052701017e85cbbd384573335de864d4769d714: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen28540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28541" type="x-p"/> The captive exile hasteneth that he may be loosed "He marcheth on with speed, who cometh to set free the captive" - Cyrus, if understood of the temporal redemption from the captivity of Babylon; in the spiritual sense, the Messiah, who comes to open the prison to them that are bound.
entries.34a26faf14b4577b1160e25499c54af8ce508d63: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen28541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28542" type="x-p"/> That I may plant the heavens "To stretch out the heavens" - In the present text it is לנתע lintoa, "to plant the heavens:" the phrase is certainly very obscure, and in all probability is a mistake for לנטות lintoth. This latter is the word used in <reference osisRef="Isa.51.13">Isa 51:13</reference> just before, in the very same sentence; and this phrase occurs very frequently in Isaiah, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.22">Isa 40:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.42.5">Isa 42:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.24">Isa 44:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.12">Isa 45:12</reference>; the former in no other place. It is also very remarkable, that in the Samaritan text, <reference osisRef="Num.24.6">Num 24:6</reference>, these two words are twice changed by mistake, one for the other, in the same verse.
entries.374d63a5f56f2db624a94cebd54d74ceff13c2ae: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen28542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28543" type="x-p"/> The cup of trembling - כוס התרעלה cos hattarelah, "the cup of mortal poison," veneni mortiferi. - Montan. This may also allude to the ancient custom of taking off criminals by a cup of poison. Socrates is well known to have been sentenced by the Areopagus to drink a cup of the juice of hemlock, which occasioned his death. See the note on <reference osisRef="Heb.2.9">Heb 2:9</reference>, and see also Bishop Lowth's note on <reference osisRef="Isa.51.21">Isa 51:21</reference>.
entries.7a2a3aeddc43573586b25b21e3268fcdd0f1b214: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen28543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28544" type="x-p"/> These two things - desolation, and destruction, and the famine, and the sword - That is, desolation by famine, and destruction by the sword, taking the terms alternately: of which form of construction see other examples. De S. Poesi, Hebrews Prael. xix., and Prelim. Dissert. p. 30. The Chaldee paraphrast, not rightly understanding this, has had recourse to the following expedient: "Two afflictions are come upon thee, and when four shall come upon thee, depredation, and destruction, and the famine, and the sword" Five MSS. הרעב haraab, without the conjunction ו vau; and so the Septuagint and Syriac. <div eID="gen28544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28545" type="x-p"/> By whom shall I comfort thee "Who shall comfort thee" - A MS., the Septuagint, Syriac, Chaldee, and Vulgate have it in the third person, ינחמך yenachamech, which is evidently right.
entries.be05b87e17044cb81173d3c675ba4d15f4e60d32: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen28545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28546" type="x-p"/> As a wild bull in a net: they are full, etc. "Like the oryx taken in the toils; drenched to the full" - "Perhaps מכמרה מלאים michmerah meleim." Secker. The demonstrative ה he, prefixed to מלאים meleim, full, seems improper in this place.
entries.9e03dc4628b80712e64c7a547ed80e4935735fbb: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen28546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28547" type="x-p"/> Drunken, but not with wine - Aeschylus has the same expression: - Αοινοις εμμανεις θυμωμασι· <div eID="gen28547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28548" type="x-p"/> Eumen. 863. <div eID="gen28548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28549" type="x-p"/> Intoxicated with passion, not with wine. <div eID="gen28549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28550" type="x-p"/> Schultens thinks that this circumlocution, as he calls it, gradum adfert incomparabiliter majorem; and that it means, not simply without wine, but much more than with wine. Gram. Hebrews p. 182. See his note on Job 30:38. <div eID="gen28550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28551" type="x-p"/> The bold image of the cup of God's wrath, often employed by the sacred writers, (see note on <reference osisRef="Isa.1.22">Isa 1:22</reference>), is nowhere handled with greater force and sublimity than in this passage of Isaiah, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.17-Isa.51.23">Isa 51:17-23</reference>. Jerusalem is represented in person as staggering under the effects of it, destitute of that assistance which she might expect from her children; not one of them being able to support or to lead her. They, abject and amazed, lie at the head of every street, overwhelmed with the greatness of their distress; like the oryx entangled in a net, in vain struggling to rend it, and extricate himself. This is poetry of the first order, sublimity of the highest character. <div eID="gen28551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28552" type="x-p"/> Plato had an idea something like this: "Suppose," says he, "God had given to men a medicating potion inducing fear, so that the more any one should drink of it, so much the more miserable he should find himself at every draught, and become fearful of every thing both present and future; and at last, though the most courageous of men, should be totally possessed by fear: and afterwards, having slept off the effects of it, should become himself again." De Leg. i., near the end. He pursues at large this hypothesis, applying it to his own purpose, which has no relation to the present subject. Homer places two vessels at the disposal of Jupiter, one of good, the other of evil. He gives to some a potion mixed of both; to others from the evil vessel only: these are completely miserable. Iliad 24:527-533. Δοιοι γαρ τε πιθοι κατακειαται εν Διος ουδει Δωρων, οἱα διδωσι, κακων, ἑτερος δε εαων, Ὡ μεν καμμιξας δῳη Ζευς τερπικεραυνος, Αλλοτε μεν τε κακῳ ὁγε κυρεται, αλλοτε δ' εσθλῳ· Ὡ δε κε των λυγρων δῳη, λωβητον εθηκε. Και ἑ κακη βουβρωστις επι χθονα διαν ελαυνει· Φοιτᾳ δ' ουτε θεοισι τετιμενος, ουτι βροτοισιν. "Two urns by Jove's high throne have ever stood, <div eID="gen28552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28553" type="x-p"/> The source of evil one, and one of good; <div eID="gen28553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28554" type="x-p"/> From thence the cup of mortal man he fills, <div eID="gen28554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28555" type="x-p"/> Blessings to these, to those distributes ills; <div eID="gen28555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28556" type="x-p"/> To most he mingles both: the wretch decreed <div eID="gen28556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28557" type="x-p"/> To taste the bad unmixed, is cursed indeed: <div eID="gen28557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28558" type="x-p"/> Pursued by wrongs, by meagre famine driven, <div eID="gen28558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28559" type="x-p"/> He wanders outcast both of earth and heaven." <div eID="gen28559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28560" type="x-p"/> Pope
entries.867c81a1f4e710778b6275bbc9292e686f25af3e: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen28560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28561" type="x-p"/> Them that afflict thee "Them who oppress thee" - The Septuagint, Chaldee, Syriac, and Vulgate appear to have read מוניך monayich, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.26">Isa 40:26</reference>." - Secker. <div eID="gen28561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28562" type="x-p"/> Which have said to thy soul, Bow down "Who say to thee, Bow down thy body" - A very strong and most expressive description of the insolent pride of eastern conquerors; which, though it may seem greatly exaggerated, yet hardly exceeds the strict truth. An example has already been given of it in the note to <reference osisRef="Isa.49.23">Isa 49:23</reference>. I will here add one or two more. "Joshua called for all the men of Israel; and said unto the captains of the men of war that went with him, Come near, put your feet upon the necks of these kings," <reference osisRef="Jos.10.24">Jos 10:24</reference>. "Adonibezek said, Threescore and ten kings, having their thumbs and their great toes cut off, gathered their meat under my table: As I have done, so hath God requited me," <reference osisRef="Jdg.1.7">Jdg 1:7</reference>. The Emperor Valerianus, being through treachery taken prisoner by Sapor king of Persia, was treated by him as the basest and most abject slave: for the Persian monarch commanded the unhappy Roman to bow himself down, and offer him his back, on which he set his foot, in order to mount his chariot or horse whenever he had occasion. - Lactantius, De Mort. Persec. cap. 5. Aurel. Victor. Epitome, cap. xxxii. - L.  <chapter eID="Isa.51"/> <div eID="gen28562" type="x-p"/>

entries.15080585d916494fc738fe002e308bc0abe0c205: <reference osisRef="Isa.51.1-Isa.51.3">Isa 51:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen13482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13483" type="x-p"/> The prophetic address now turns again from the despisers of the word, whom it has threatened with the torment of fire, to those who long for salvation. <hi type="italic">“Hearken to me, ye that are in pursuit of righteousness, ye that seek Jehovah. Look up to the rock whence ye are hewn, and to the hollow of the pit whence ye are dug. Look up toe Abraham your forefather, and to Sara who bare you, that he was one when I called him, and blessed him, and multiplied him. For Jehovah hath comforted Zion, comforted all her ruins, and turned her desert like Eden, and her steppe as into the garden of God; joy and gladness are found in her, thanksgiving and sounding music.”</hi> The prophecy is addressed to those who are striving after the right kind of life and seeking Jehovah, and not turning from Him to make earthly things and themselves the object of their pursuit; for such only are in a condition by faith to regard that as possible, and in spirit to behold that as real, which seems impossible, and in spirit to behold that as real, which seems impossible to human understanding, because the very opposite is lying before the eye of the senses. Abraham and Sarah they are mentally to set before them, for they are types of the salvation to be anticipated now. Abraham is the rock whence the stones were hewn, of which the house of Jacob is composed; and Sarah with her maternal womb the hollow of the pit out of which Israel was brought to the light, just as peat is dug out of a pit, or copper out of a mine. The marriage of Abraham and Sarah was for a long time unfruitful; it was, as it were, out of hard stone that God raised up children to Himself in Abraham and Sarah. The rise of Israel was a miracle of divine power and grace. In antithesis to the masculine <hi type="italic">tsūr</hi>, <hi type="italic">bōr</hi> is made into a feminine through <hi type="italic">maqqebheth</hi>, which is chosen with reference to <hi type="italic">neqēbhâh</hi>. to חצּבתּם we must supply ממּנּוּ ... אשׁר, and to נקּרתּם, ממּנּה ... אשׁר. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.51.2">Isa 51:2</reference></hi> informs them who the rock and the hollow of the pit are, viz., Abraham your forefather, and Sarah <hi type="italic">techōlelkhem</hi>, who bare you with all the pains of childbirth: “<hi type="italic">you</hi>,” for the birth of Isaac, the son of promise, was the birth of the nation. The point to be specially looked at in relation to Abraham (in comparison with whom Sarah falls into the background) is given in the words <hi type="italic">quod unum vocavi eum</hi> (that he was one when I called him). The perfect קראתיו relates the single call of divine grace, which removed Abraham from the midst of idolaters into the fellowship of Jehovah. The futures that follow (with <hi type="italic">Vav cop.</hi>) point out the blessing and multiplication that were connected with it (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.1-Gen.12.2">Gen 12:1-2</reference>). He is called one (<hi type="italic">'echâd</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.24">Eze 33:24</reference>; Mal 2:15), because he was one at the time of his call, and yet through the might of the divine blessing became the root of the whole genealogical tree of Israel, and of a great multitude of people that branched off from it. This is what those who are now longing for salvation are to remember, strengthening themselves by means of the olden time in their faith in the future which so greatly resembles it. The corresponding blessing is expressed in preterites (<hi type="italic">nicham</hi>, <hi type="italic">vayyâsem</hi>), inasmuch as to the eye of faith and in prophetic vision the future has the reality of a present and the certainty of a completed fact. Zion, the mother of Israel (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.1">Isa 50:1</reference>), the counterpart of Sarah, the ancestress of the nation-Zion, which is now mourning so bitterly, because she is lying waste and in ruins - is comforted by Jehovah. The comforting word of promise (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.1">Isa 40:1</reference>) becomes, in her case, the comforting fact of fulfilment (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.13">Isa 49:13</reference>). Jehovah makes her waste like Eden (lxx ὡς παράδεισον), like a garden, as glorious as if it had been directly planted by Himself (<reference osisRef="Gen.13.10">Gen 13:10</reference>; Num 24:6). And this paradise is not without human occupants; but when you enter it you find joy and gladness therein, and hear thanksgiving at the wondrous change that has taken place, as well as the voice of melody (<hi type="italic">zimrâh</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Amos.5.23">Amo 5:23</reference>). The pleasant land is therefore full of men in the midst of festal enjoyment and activity. As Sarah gave birth to Isaac after a long period of barrenness, so Zion, a second Sarah, will be surrounded by a joyous multitude of children after a long period of desolation.
entries.50a19701905415c21b1be21b661b1639971e5eda: <reference osisRef="Isa.51.4-Isa.51.5">Isa 51:4-5</reference> <div eID="gen13483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13484" type="x-p"/> But the great work of the future extends far beyond the restoration of Israel, which becomes the source of salvation to all the world. <hi type="italic">“Hearken unto me, my people, and give ear unto me, O my congregation! for instruction will go forth from me, and I make a place for my right, to be a light of the nations. My righteousness is near, my salvation is drawn out, and my arms will judge nations: the hoping of the islands looks to me, and for mine arm is their waiting.”</hi> It is Israel which is here summoned to hearken to the promise introduced with <hi type="italic">kı̄</hi>. לאוּמּי is only used here of Israel, like גּוי in Zep 2:9; and the lxx (καὶ οἱ βασιλεῖς) have quite misunderstood it. An address to the heathen would be quite out of harmony with the character of the whole prophecy, which is carried out quite consistently throughout. עמי and לאומי, therefore, are not plurals, as the Syriac supposes, although it cannot be disputed that it is a rare thing to meet with the plural form apocopated thus, after the form of the talmudic Aramaean; and see also at <reference osisRef="Ps.45.9">Psa 45:9</reference>). What Isa 42:1. describes as the calling of the servant of Jehovah, viz., to carry out justice among the nations, and to plant it on the earth, appears here as the act of Jehovah; but, as a comparison of מאתּי with מצּיּון (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">Isa 2:3</reference>) clearly shows, as the act of the God who is present in Israel, and works from Israel outwards. Out of Israel sprang the Saviour; out of Israel the apostleship; and when God shall have mercy upon Israel again, it will become to the whole world of nations “life from the dead.” The <hi type="italic">thorâh</hi> referred to here is that of Sion, as distinguished from that of Sinai, the gospel of redemption, and <hi type="italic">mishpât</hi> the new order of life in which Israel and the nations are united. Jehovah makes for this a place of rest, a firm standing-place, from which its light to lighten the nations streams forth in all directions. הרגּיע as in <reference osisRef="Jer.31.2">Jer 31:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.34">Jer 50:34</reference>, from רגע, in the sense of the Arabic <hi type="italic">rj‛</hi>, to return, to procure return, entrance, and rest; a different word from רגע in <reference osisRef="Isa.51.15">Isa 51:15</reference>, which signifies the very opposite, viz., to disturb, literally to throw into trembling. צדק and ישע, which occur in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.51.5">Isa 51:5</reference></hi>, are synonyms throughout these prophecies. The meaning of the former is determined by the character of the <hi type="italic">thorah</hi>, which gives “the knowledge of salvation” (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.77">Luk 1:77</reference>), and with that “the righteousness of God” (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.17">Rom 1:17</reference>; cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.53.11">Isa 53:11</reference>). This righteousness is now upon the point of being revealed; this salvation has started on the way towards the fullest realization. The great mass of the nations fall under the judgment which the arms of Jehovah inflict, as they cast down to the ground on the right hand and on the left. When it is stated of the islands, therefore, that they hope for Jehovah, and wait for His arm, the reference is evidently to the remnant of the heathen nations, which outlives the judgment, and not only desires salvation, and is susceptible of it, but which actually receives salvation (compare the view given in Joh 11:52, which agrees with that of Isaiah, and which, in fact, is the biblical view generally, e.g., <reference osisRef="Joel.3.5">Joe 3:5</reference>). To these the saving arm (the singular only was suitable here; cf., <reference osisRef="Ps.16.11">Psa 16:11</reference>) now brings that salvation, towards which their longing was more or less consciously directed, and which satisfied their inmost need. Observe in <reference osisRef="Isa.51.5">Isa 51:5</reference> the majestic and self-conscious movement of the rhythm, with the effective tone of <hi type="italic">yeyachēlûn</hi>.
entries.b27429bf2fa6080c98658dc45dbff1b84b69a1a6: <reference osisRef="Isa.51.6">Isa 51:6</reference> <div eID="gen13484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13485" type="x-p"/> The people of God are now summoned to turn their eyes upwards and downwards: the old world above their heads and under their feet is destined to destruction. <hi type="italic">“Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look upon the earth beneath: for the heavens will pass away like smoke, and the earth fall to pieces like a garment, and its inhabitants die out like a nonentity; and my salvation will last for ever, and my righteousness does not go to ruin.”</hi> The reason for the summons follows with <hi type="italic">kı̄</hi>. The heavens will be resolved into atoms, like smoke: <hi type="italic">nimlâchū</hi> from <hi type="italic">mâlach</hi>, related to <hi type="italic">mârach</hi>, root <hi type="italic">mal</hi>, from which comes <hi type="italic">mâlal</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Job.14.2">Job 14:2</reference>), to rub to pieces, to crumble to pieces, or mangle; Aquila, ἠλοήθησαν, from ἀλοᾶν, to thresh. As <hi type="italic">melâchı̄m</hi> signifies rags, the figure of a garment that has fallen to pieces, which was then quite ready to hand (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.9">Isa 50:9</reference>), presented itself from the natural association of ideas. כּמו־כן, however, cannot mean “in like manner” (lxx, Targ., Jerome); for if we keep to the figure of a garment falling to pieces, the figure is a very insipid one; and if we refer it to the fate of the earth generally, the thought which it offers is a very tame one. The older expositors were not even acquainted with what is now the favourite explanation, viz., “as gnats perish” (Hitzig, Ewald, Umbreit, Knobel, Stier, etc.); since the singular of <hi type="italic">kinnı̄m</hi> is no more <hi type="italic">kēn</hi> than the singular of בּיצים is בּיץ. The gnat (viz., a species of stinging gnat, probably the diminutive but yet very troublesome species which is called <hi type="italic">akol uskut</hi>, “eat and be silent,” in Egyptian) is called <hi type="italic">kinnâh</hi>, as the talmudic usage shows, where the singular, which does not happen to be met with in the Old Testament, is found in the case of <hi type="italic">kinnı̄m</hi> as well as in that of <hi type="italic">bētsı̄m</hi>.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Kinnâm</hi>, in <reference osisRef="Exod.8.13-Exod.8.14">Exo 8:13-14</reference>, whether it be a collective plural or a singular, also proves nothing in support of <hi type="italic">kēn</hi>, any more than <hi type="italic">middâh</hi> in <reference osisRef="Job.11.9">Job 11:9</reference> (which see) in favour of <hi type="italic">mad</hi>, in the sense of measure. It does not follow, that because a certain form lies at the foundation of a derivative, it must have been current in ordinary usage.</note> <div eID="gen13485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13486" type="x-p"/> We must explain the word in the same manner as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.5">2Sa 23:5</reference>; Num 13:33; Job 9:35. In all these passages <hi type="italic">kēn</hi> merely signifies “so” (<hi type="italic">ita</hi>,<hi type="italic">sic</hi>); but just as in the classical languages, these words often derive their meaning from the gesture with which they are accompanied (e.g., in Terence’s <hi type="italic">Eunuch: Cape hoc flabellum et ventulum sic facito</hi>). This is probably Rückert’s opinion, when he adopts the rendering: and its inhabitants “like so” (<hi type="italic">so</hi> <hi type="italic">wie</hi> <hi type="italic">so</hi>) do they die. But “like so” is here equivalent to “like nothing.” That the heavens and the earth do not perish without rising again in a renewed form, is a thought which may naturally be supplied, and which is distinctly expressed in <reference osisRef="Isa.51.16">Isa 51:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.17">Isa 65:17</reference>; Isa 66:22. Righteousness (<hi type="italic">tsedâqâh</hi>) and salvation (<hi type="italic">yeshū‛âh</hi>) are the heavenly powers, which acquire dominion through the overthrow of the ancient world, and become the foundations of the new (2Pe 3:13). That the <hi type="italic">tsedâqâh</hi> will endure for ever, and the <hi type="italic">yeshū‛âh</hi> will not be broken (<hi type="italic">yēchath</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.7.8">Isa 7:8</reference>, <hi type="italic">confringetur</hi>, whereas in <reference osisRef="Isa.51.7">Isa 51:7</reference> the meaning is <hi type="italic">consternemini</hi>), is a prospect that opens after the restoration of the new world, and which indirectly applies to men who survive the catastrophe, having become partakers of righteousness and salvation. For righteousness and salvation require beings in whom to exert their power.
entries.384f6ebdddff4f3c1e7dd946b60210a5774acd84: <reference osisRef="Isa.51.7-Isa.51.8">Isa 51:7-8</reference> <div eID="gen13486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13487" type="x-p"/> Upon this magnificent promise of the final triumph of the counsel of God, an exhortation is founded to the persecuted church, not to be afraid of men. <hi type="italic">“Hearken unto me, ye that know about righteousness, thou people with my law in the heart; fear ye not the reproach of mortals, and be ye not alarmed at their revilings. For the moth will devour them like a garment, and the worm devour them like woollen cloth; and my righteousness will stand for ever, and my salvation to distant generations.”</hi> The idea of the “servant of Jehovah,” in its middle sense, viz., as denoting the true Israel, is most clearly set forth in the address here. They that pursue after righteousness, and seek Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.1">Isa 51:1</reference>), that is to say, the servants of Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.8-Isa.65.9">Isa 65:8-9</reference>), are embraced in the unity of a “people,” as in <reference osisRef="Isa.65.10">Isa 65:10</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.10.24">Isa 10:24</reference>), i.e., of the true people of God in the people of His choice, and therefore of the kernel in the heart of the whole mass - an integral intermediate link in the organism of the general idea, which Hävernick and, to a certain extent, Hofmann eliminate from it,<note placement="foot">Hävernick, in his <hi type="italic">Lectures on the Theology of the Old Testament</hi>, published by H. A. Hahn, 1848, and in a second edition by H. Schultz, 1863; Drechsler, in his article on the Servant of Jehovah, in the <hi type="italic">Luth. Zeitschrift</hi>, 1852; V. Hofmann, in his <hi type="italic">Schriftbeweis</hi>, ii. 1, 147. The first two understand by the servant of Jehovah as an individual, the true Israel personified: the idea has simply Israel as a whole at its base, i.e., Israel which did not answer to its ideal, and the Messiah as the summit, in whom the ideal of Israel was fully realized. Drechsler goes so far as to call the central link, viz., an Israel true to its vocation, a modern abstraction that has no support in the Scriptures. Hofmann, however, says that he has no wish to exclude this central idea, and merely wishes to guard against the notion that a number of individuals, whether Israelites generally or pious Israelites, are ever intended by the epithet “servant of Jehovah.” “The nation,” he says himself at p. 145, “was called as a nation to be the servant of God, but it fulfilled its calling as a church of believers.” And so say we; but we also add that this church is a kernel always existing within the outer <hi type="italic">ecclesia mixta</hi>, and therefore always a number of individuals, though they are only known to God.</note> but not without thereby destroying the typical mirror in which the prophet beholds the passion of the One. The words are addressed to those who know from their own experience what righteousness is as a gift of grace, and as conduct in harmony with the plan of salvation, i.e., to the nation, which bears in its heart the law of God as the standard and impulse of its life, the church which not only has it as a letter outside itself, but as a vital power within (cf., <reference osisRef="Ps.40.9">Psa 40:9</reference>). None of these need to be afraid of men. Their despisers and blasphemers are men (<hi type="italic">'ĕnōsh</hi>; cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.51.12">Isa 51:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.9.20">Psa 9:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.10.18">Psa 10:18</reference>), whose pretended omnipotence, exaltation, and indestructibility, are an unnatural self-convicted lie. The double figure in <reference osisRef="Isa.51.8">Isa 51:8</reference>, which forms a play upon words that cannot well be reproduced, affirms that the smallest exertion of strength is quite sufficient to annihilate their sham greatness and sham power; and that long before they are actually destroyed, they carry the constantly increasing germ of it within themselves. The <hi type="italic">sâs</hi>, says a Jewish proverb, is brother to the <hi type="italic">‛âsh</hi>. The latter (from <hi type="italic">‛âshēsh</hi>, <hi type="italic">collabi</hi>, Arab. <hi type="italic">‛aththa</hi>, trans. <hi type="italic">corrodere</hi>) signifies a moth; the former (like the Arabic <hi type="italic">sūs</hi>, <hi type="italic">sūse</hi>, Gr. σής) a moth, and also a weevil, <hi type="italic">curculio</hi>. The relative terms in Greek are σής (Armen. <hi type="italic">tzetz</hi>) and κίς. But whilst the persecutors of the church succumb to these powers of destruction, the righteousness and salvation of God, which are even now the confidence and hope of His church, and the full and manifest realization of which it will hereafter enjoy, stand for ever, and from “generation to generation,” <hi type="italic">ledōr dōrı̄m</hi>, i.e., to an age which embraces endless ages within itself.
entries.d287a6adeb0d9cbad30e54533812571e71de3157: <reference osisRef="Isa.51.9-Isa.51.11">Isa 51:9-11</reference> <div eID="gen13487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13488" type="x-p"/> But just as such an exhortation as this followed very naturally from the grand promises with which they prophecy commenced, so does a longing for the promised salvation spring out of this exhortation, together with the assurance of its eventual realization. <hi type="italic">“Awake, awake, clothe thyself in might, O arm of Jehovah; awake, as in the days of ancient time, the ages of the olden world! Was it not thou that didst split Rahab in pieces, and pierced the dragon? Was it not thou that didst dry up the sea, the waters of the great billow; that didst turn the depths of the sea into a way for redeemed to pass through? Ad the emancipated of Jehovah will return, and come to Zion with shouting, and everlasting joy upon their head: they grasp at gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing flee away.”</hi> The paradisaical restoration of Zion, the new world of righteousness and salvation, is a work of the arm of Jehovah, i.e., of the manifestation of His might. His arm is now in a sleeping state. It is not lifeless, indeed, but motionless. Therefore the church calls out to it three times, “Awake” (<hi type="italic">‛ūrı̄</hi>: to avoid monotony, the <hi type="italic">milra</hi> and <hi type="italic">milel</hi> tones are interchanged, as in Jdg 5:12).<note placement="foot">See Norzi and Luzzatto’s <hi type="italic">Grammatica della Lingua Ebr</hi>. §513.</note> <div eID="gen13488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13489" type="x-p"/> It is to arise and put on strength out of the fulness of omnipotence (<hi type="italic">lâbhēsh</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Ps.93.1">Psa 93:1</reference>; cf., λαμβάνειν δύναμιν <reference osisRef="Rev.11.17">Rev 11:17</reference>, and δύσεο ἀλκήν, arm thyself with strength, in <hi type="italic">Il</hi>. 19:36; 9:231). The arm of Jehovah is able to accomplish what the prophecy affirms and the church hopes for; since it has already miraculously redeemed Israel once. <hi type="italic">Rahabh</hi> is Egypt represented as a monster of the waters (see <reference osisRef="Isa.30.7">Isa 30:7</reference>), and <hi type="italic">tannı̄n</hi> is the same (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Isa 27:1</reference>), but with particular reference to Pharaoh (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.3">Eze 29:3</reference>). אתּ־היא, <hi type="italic">tu</hi> <hi type="italic">illud</hi>, is equivalent to “thou, yea thou” (see at <reference osisRef="Isa.37.16">Isa 37:16</reference>). The Red Sea is described as the “waters of the great deep” (<hi type="italic">tehōm</hi> <hi type="italic">rabbâh</hi>), because the great storehouse of waters that lie below the solid ground were partially manifested there. השּׂמה has double <hi type="italic">pashta</hi>; it is therefore <hi type="italic">milel</hi>, and therefore the third pr. = שׂמה אשׁר (Ges. §109, Anf.). <reference osisRef="Isa.35.10">Isa 35:10</reference> is repeated in <reference osisRef="Isa.51.11">Isa 51:11</reference>, being attached to גּאוּלים of the previous verse, jut as it is there. Instead of נסוּ ישּׂיגוּן, which we find here, we have there ונסוּ ישּׂיגוּ; in everything else the two passages are word for word the same. Hitzig, Ewald, and Knobel suppose that <reference osisRef="Isa.51.11">Isa 51:11</reference> was not written by the author of these addresses, but was interpolated by some one else. But in <reference osisRef="Isa.65.25">Isa 65:25</reference> we meet with just the same kind of repetition from chapters 1-39; and in the first part we find, at any rate, repetitions in the form of refrains and others of a smaller kind (like <reference osisRef="Isa.19.15">Isa 19:15</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.9.13">Isa 9:13</reference>). And <reference osisRef="Isa.51.11">Isa 51:11</reference> forms a conclusion here, just as it does in Isa 35:10. An argument is founded upon the olden time with reference to the things to be expected now; the look into the future is cleared and strengthened by the look into the past. And thus will the emancipated of Jehovah return, being liberated from the present calamity as they were delivered from the Egyptian then. The first half of this prophecy is here brought to a close. It concludes with expressions of longing and of hope, the echo of promises that had gone before.
entries.00bb09fc682d7f57f6153000e0c6c8aab98d6824: <reference osisRef="Isa.51.12-Isa.51.15">Isa 51:12-15</reference> <div eID="gen13489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13490" type="x-p"/> In the second half the promise commences again, but with more distinct reference to the oppression of the exiles and the sufferings of Jerusalem. Jehovah Himself begins to speak now, setting His seal upon what is longed and hoped for. <hi type="italic">“I am your comforter: who art thou, that thou shouldst be afraid of a mortal who will die, and of a son of man who is made a blade of grass; that thou shouldst forget Jehovah thy Creator, who stretched out the heavens and founded the earth; that thou shouldst be afraid continually all the day of the fury of the tormentor, as he aims to destroy? and where is the fury of the tormentor left? He that is bowed down is quickly set loose, and does not die to the grave, and his bread does not fail him; as truly as I Jehovah am thy God, who frighteneth up the sea, so that its waves roar: Jehovah of hosts is His name.”</hi> הוּא after אנכי אנכי is an emphatic repetition, and therefore a strengthening of the subject (αὐτὸς ἐγώ), as above, in <reference osisRef="Isa.51.10">Isa 51:10</reference>, in אתּ־היא. From this major, that Jehovah is the comforter of His church, and by means of a minor, that whoever has Him for a comforter has no need to fear, the conclusion is drawn that the church has no cause to fear. Consequently we cannot adopt Knobel’s explanation, “How small thou art, that thou art afraid.” The meaning is rather, “Is it really the case with thee (i.e., art thou then so small, so forsaken), that thou hast any need to fear” (fut. consec., according to Ges. §129, 1; cf., <hi type="italic">ki</hi>, <reference osisRef="Exod.3.11">Exo 3:11</reference>; Jdg 9:28)? The attributive sentence <hi type="italic">tâmūth</hi> (who will die) brings out the meaning involved in the epithet applied to man, viz., <hi type="italic">'ĕnōsh</hi> (compare in the Persian myth <hi type="italic">Gayomard</hi>, from the old Persian <hi type="italic">gaya meretan</hi>, mortal life); חציר = כּחציר (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.2">Psa 37:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.90.5">Psa 90:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.103.15">Psa 103:15</reference>; compare above, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.6-Isa.40.8">Isa 40:6-8</reference>) is an equation instead of a comparison. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.51.12">Isa 51:12</reference></hi> the address is thrown into a feminine form, in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.51.13">Isa 51:13</reference></hi> into a masculine one; Zion being the object in the former, and (what is the same thing) Israel in the latter: that thou forgettest thy Creator, who is also the almighty Maker of the universe, and soarest about in constant endless alarm at the wrath of the tormentor, whilst he is aiming to destroy (<hi type="italic">pichad</hi>, <hi type="italic">contremiscere</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Prov.28.14">Pro 28:14</reference>; <hi type="italic">ka'ăsher</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Ps.66.7">Psa 66:7</reference>; Num 27:14, lit., according as; <hi type="italic">kōnēn</hi>, viz., his arrows, or even his bow, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.11.2">Psa 11:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.7.13">Psa 7:13</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.21.13">Isa 21:13</reference>). We must not translate this <hi type="italic">quasi disposuisset</hi>, which is opposed to the actual fact, although syntactically possible (<reference osisRef="Job.10.19">Job 10:19</reference>; Zec 10:6). The question with which the fear is met, “And where is the fury of the tormentor?” looks into the future: “There is not a trace of him to be seen, he is utterly swept away.” If <hi type="italic">hammētsı̄q</hi> signifies the Chaldean, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.14">Isa 51:14</reference>, in which the warning passes into a promise, just as in the first half the promise passed into a warning, is not to be understood as referring to oppression by their own countrymen, who were more heathenish than Israelitish in their disposition, as Knobel supposes; but <hi type="italic">tsō‛eh</hi> (from <hi type="italic">tsâ‛âh</hi>, to stoop or bend) is an individualizing description of the exiles, who were in captivity in Babylon, and some of them actually in prison (see <reference osisRef="Isa.42.7">Isa 42:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.42.22">Isa 42:22</reference>). Those who were lying there in fetters, and were therefore obliged to bend, hastened to be loosed, i.e., would speedily be set at liberty (the conquest of Babylon by Cyrus may be referred to here); they would not die and fall into the pit (<hi type="italic">constr. praegnans</hi>), nor would their bread fail; that is to say, if we regard the two clauses as the dissection of one thought (which is not necessary, however, though Hitzig supports it), “he will not die of starvation.” The pledge of this is to be found in the all-sufficiency of Jehovah, who throws the sea into a state of trembling (even by a threatening word, <hi type="italic">geârâh</hi>; רגע is the construct of the participle, with the tone upon the last syllable, as in <reference osisRef="Lev.11.7">Lev 11:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.94.9">Psa 94:9</reference> : see Bär’s <hi type="italic">Psalter</hi>, p. 132, from <hi type="italic">râga‛</hi>, <hi type="italic">tremefacere</hi>), so that its waves roar (cf., <reference osisRef="Jer.31.35">Jer 31:35</reference>, and the original passage in <reference osisRef="Job.26.12">Job 26:12</reference>).
entries.4d7e0f03c646067044904671446ec25e125c527a: <reference osisRef="Isa.51.16">Isa 51:16</reference> <div eID="gen13490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13491" type="x-p"/> The promise, as the pledge of which Jehovah has staked His absolute power, to which everything must yield, now rises up to an eschatological height, from the historical point at which it began. <hi type="italic">“And I put my words into thy mouth, and in the shadow of my hand have I covered thee, to plant heavens, and to found an earth, and to say to Zion, Thou art my people.”</hi> It is a lofty calling, a glorious future, for the preparation and introduction of which Israel, although fallen as low as <reference osisRef="Isa.51.7">Isa 51:7</reference> describes, has been equipped and kept in the shadow of unapproachable omnipotence. Jehovah has put His words into the mouth of this Israel - His words, the force and certainty of which are measured by His all-determining absoluteness. And what is the exalted calling which it is to subserve through the medium of these words, and for which it is preserved, without previously, or indeed at any time, passing away? We must not render it, “that thou mayest plant,” etc., with which the conclusion does not harmonize, viz., “that thou mayest say,” etc.; for it is not Israel who says this to Israel, but Jehovah says it to Israel. The planter, founder, speaker, is therefore Jehovah. It is God’s own work, to which Israel is merely instrumentally subservient, by means of the words of God place din its mouth, viz., the new creation of the world, and the restoration of Israel to favour; both of them, the former as well as the latter, <hi type="italic">regalia</hi> of God. The reference is to the last times. The Targum explains it thus: “to restore the people of whom it is said, They will be as numerous as the stars of heaven; and to perfect the church, of which it is said, They will be as numerous as the dust of the earth.” Knobel understands by this a completion of the theocracy, and a new arrangement of the condition of the world; Ewald, a new spiritual creation, of which the liberation of Israel is the first corner-stone. But the prophecy speaks of a new heaven and a new earth, in something more than a figurative sense, as a new creation of God (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.17">Isa 65:17</reference>). Jehovah intends to create a new world of righteousness and salvation, and practically to acknowledge Zion as His people. The preparation for this great and all-renewing work of the future is aided by the true Israel, which is now enslaved by the heathen, and disowned and persecuted by its own countrymen. A future of salvation, embracing Israel and the heaven and the earth, is implied in the words placed by Jehovah in the mouth of His church, which was faithful to its calling. These words in their mouth are the seed-corns of a new world in the midst of the old. The fact that the very same thing is said here of the true spiritual Israel, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.49.2">Isa 49:2</reference> of the one servant of Jehovah, may be explained in the same manner as when the apostles apply to themselves, in <reference osisRef="Acts.13.47">Act 13:47</reference>, a word of God relating to the one Servant of Jehovah, by saying, “So hath the Lord commanded us.” The One is, in fact, one with this Israel; He is this Israel in its highest potency; He towers above it, but only as the head rises above the members of the body, with which it forms a living whole. There is no necessity, therefore, to assume, as Hengstenberg and Philippi do, that <reference osisRef="Isa.51.13">Isa 51:13</reference> contains an address from the One who then stood before the mind of the prophet. “There is no proof,” as Vitringa affirms, “of any change in the object in this passage, nor any solid reason for assuming it.” The circumference of the idea is always the same. Here, however, it merely takes the direction towards the centre, and penetrates its smaller inner circle, but does not go back to the centre itself.
entries.77e62499424526711dc4aaa473a060f2b7e310b6: <reference osisRef="Isa.51.17-Isa.51.23">Isa 51:17-23</reference> <div eID="gen13491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13492" type="x-p"/> Just as we found above, that the exclamation “awake” (<hi type="italic">‛ūrı̄</hi>), which the church addresses to the arm of Jehovah, grew out of the preceding great promises; so here there grows out of the same another “awake” (<hi type="italic">hith‛ōrerı̄</hi>), which the prophet addresses to Jerusalem in the name of his God, and the reason for which is given in the form of new promises. <hi type="italic">“Wake thyself up, wake thyself up, stand up, O Jerusalem, thou that hast drunk out of the hand of Jehovah the goblet of His fury: the goblet cup of reeling hast thou drunk, sipped out. There was none who guided her of all the children that she had brought forth; and none who took her by the hand of all the children that she had brought up. There were two things that happened to thee; who should console thee? Devastation, and ruin, and famine, and the sword: how should I comfort thee? Thy children were benighted, lay at the corners of all the streets like a snared antelope: as those who were full of the fury of Jehovah, the rebuke of thy God. Therefore hearken to this, O wretched and drunken, but not with wine: Thus saith thy Lord, Jehovah, and thy God that defendeth His people, Behold, I take out of thine hand the goblet of reeling, the goblet cup of my fury: thou shalt not continue to drink it any more. And I put it into the hand of thy tormentors; who said to thy soul, Bow down, that we may go over; and thou madest thy back like the ground, and like a public way for those who go over it.”</hi> In <reference osisRef="Isa.51.17">Isa 51:17</reference>, Jerusalem is regarded as a woman lying on the ground in the sleep of faintness and stupefaction. She has been obliged to drink, for her punishment, the goblet filled with the fury of the wrath of God, the goblet which throws those who drink it into unconscious reeling; and this goblet, which is called <hi type="italic">qubba‛ath</hi> <hi type="italic">kōs</hi> (κύπελλον ποτηιρίου, a genitive construction, though appositional in sense), for the purpose of giving greater prominence to its swelling sides, she has not only had to drink, but to drain quite clean (cf., <reference osisRef="Ps.75.9">Psa 75:9</reference>, and more especially <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.32-Ezek.23.34">Eze 23:32-34</reference>). Observe the plaintive falling of the tone in <hi type="italic">shâthı̄th</hi> <hi type="italic">mâtsı̄th</hi>. In this state of unconscious stupefaction was Jerusalem lying, without any help on the part of her children; there was not one who came to guide the stupefied one, or took her by the hand to lift her up. The consciousness of the punishment that their sins had deserved, and the greatness of the sufferings that the punishment had brought, pressed so heavily upon all the members of the congregation, that not one of them showed the requisite cheerfulness and strength to rise up on her behalf, so as to make her fate at any rate tolerable to her, and ward off the worst calamities. What elegiac music we have here in the deep cadences: <hi type="italic">mikkol</hi>-<hi type="italic">bânı̄m</hi> <hi type="italic">yâlâdâh</hi>, <hi type="italic">mikkol</hi>-<hi type="italic">bânı̄m</hi> <hi type="italic">giddēlâh !</hi> So terrible was her calamity, that no one ventured to break the silence of the terror, or give expression to their sympathy. Even the prophet, humanly speaking, is obliged to exclaim, “How (<hi type="italic">mı̄</hi>, literally as who, as in <reference osisRef="Amos.7.2">Amo 7:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.7.5">Amo 7:5</reference>) should I comfort thee!” He knew of no equal or greater calamity, to which he could point Jerusalem, according to the principle which experience confirms, <hi type="italic">solamen miseris socios habuisse malorum</hi>. This is the real explanation, according to <reference osisRef="Lam.2.13">Lam 2:13</reference>, though we must not therefore take <hi type="italic">mı̄</hi> as an accusative = <hi type="italic">bemı̄</hi>, as Hitzig does. The whole of the group is in the tone of the Lamentations of Jeremiah. There were two kinds of things (i.e., two kinds of evils: <hi type="italic">mishpâchōth</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.15.3">Jer 15:3</reference>) that had happened to her (קרא = קרה, with which it is used interchangeably even in the Pentateuch) - namely, the devastation and ruin of their city and their land, famine and the sword to her children, their inhabitants. <div eID="gen13492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13493" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Isa.51.20">Isa 51:20</reference> this is depicted with special reference to the famine. Her children were veiled (<hi type="italic">‛ullaph</hi>, <hi type="italic">deliquium pati</hi>, lit., <hi type="italic">obvelari</hi>), and lay in a state of unconsciousness like corpses at the corner of every street, where this horrible spectacle presented itself on every hand. They lay <hi type="italic">ketho'</hi> <hi type="italic">mikhmâr</hi> (rendered strangely and with very bad taste in the lxx, viz., like a half-cooked turnip; but given correctly by Jerome, <hi type="italic">sicut oryx</hi>, as in the lxx at <reference osisRef="Deut.14.5">Deu 14:5</reference>, <hi type="italic">illaqueatus</hi>), i.e., like a netted antelope (see at <reference osisRef="Job.39.9">Job 39:9</reference>), i.e., one that has been taken in a hunter’s net and lies there exhausted, after having almost strangled itself by ineffectual attempts to release itself. The appositional וגו המלאים, which refers to בניך, gives as a <hi type="italic">quippe qui</hi> the reason for all this suffering. It is the punishment decreed by God, which has pierced their very heart, and got them completely in its power. This clause assigning the reason, shows that the expression “thy children” (<hi type="italic">bânayikh</hi>) is not to be taken here in the same manner as in <reference osisRef="Lam.2.11-Lam.2.12">Lam 2:11-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.4.3-Lam.4.4">Lam 4:3-4</reference>, viz., as referring to children in distinction from adults; the subject is a general one, as in Isa 5:25. With <hi type="italic">lâkhē̄n</hi> (therefore, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.21">Isa 51:21</reference>) the address turns from the picture of sufferings to the promise, in the view of which the cry was uttered, in <reference osisRef="Isa.51.17">Isa 51:17</reference>, to awake and arise. Therefore, viz., because she had endured the full measure of God’s wrath, she is to hear what His mercy, that has now begun to move, purposes to do. The connecting form <hi type="italic">shekhurath</hi> stands here, according to Ges. §116, 1, notwithstanding the (epexegetical) <hi type="italic">Vav</hi> which comes between. We may see from <reference osisRef="Isa.29.9">Isa 29:9</reference> how thoroughly this “drunk, but not with wine,” is in Isaiah’s own style (from this distinction between a higher and lower sphere of related facts, compare <reference osisRef="Isa.47.14">Isa 47:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.48.10">Isa 48:10</reference>). The intensive plural <hi type="italic">'ădōnı̄m</hi> is only applied to human lords in other places in the book of Isaiah; but in this passage, in which Jerusalem is described as a woman, it is used once of Jehovah. <hi type="italic">Yârı̄bh</hi> <hi type="italic">‛ammō</hi> is an attributive clause, signifying “who conducts the cause of His people,” i.e., their advocate or defender. He takes the goblet of reeling and wrath, which Jerusalem has emptied, for ever out of her hand, and forces it newly filled upon her tormentors. There is no ground whatever for reading מוניך (from ינה, to throw down, related to יון, whence comes יון, a precipitate or sediment) in the place of מוגי (<hi type="italic">pret. hi.</hi> of יגה, (<hi type="italic">laborare</hi>, <hi type="italic">dolere</hi>), that favourite word of the Lamentations of Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Lam.1.5">Lam 1:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.1.12">Lam 1:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.32">Lam 3:32</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.1.4">Isa 1:4</reference>), the tone of which we recognise here throughout, as Lowth, Ewald, and Umbreit propose after the Targum ליך מונן דהוו. The words attributed to the enemies, <hi type="italic">shechı̄</hi> <hi type="italic">vena‛ăbhorâh</hi> (from <hi type="italic">shâchâh</hi>, the <hi type="italic">kal</hi> of which only occurs here), are to be understood figuratively, as in Psa 129:3. Jerusalem has been obliged to let her children be degraded into the defenceless objects of despotic tyranny and caprice, both at home in their own conquered country, and abroad in exile. But the relation is reversed now. Jerusalem is delivered, after having been punished, and the instruments of her punishment are given up to the punishment which their pride deserved.  <chapter eID="Isa.51"/> <div eID="gen13493" type="x-p"/>
